lessons.title: LVM: physical volumes, volume groups, logical volumes
lessons.goal:
Learn the three layers of LVM and use them: build a volume, put a file system on it, and **grow it while mounted**.

Why it matters: LVM lets you resize storage, combine disks and take snapshots without repartitioning. Most enterprise Linux servers (including this one) have their root file system on LVM.

setup.note: These steps use sudo and loop devices (image files acting as disks). They create a volume group called `labvg` and remove it at the end. They never touch real disks.

steps.title: Three layers
steps.text:
- **PV** (physical volume): a disk or partition prepared for LVM.
- **VG** (volume group): a pool made from one or more PVs.
- **LV** (logical volume): a slice of the pool that looks like a disk. You put a file system on it.

Our practice "disks" are two 100 MB loop devices.

run.cmd: truncate -s 100M p1.img p2.img; L1=$(sudo losetup -f --show p1.img); L2=$(sudo losetup -f --show p2.img); echo $L1 $L2

run.output:
Physical volume "PV" successfully created.
  Physical volume "PV" successfully created.
  Not creating system devices file due to existing VGs.

Not creating system devices file due to existing VGs.
  Volume group "labvg" successfully created

VG    #PV #LV #SN Attr   VSize   VFree  
  labvg   2   0   0 wz--n- 192.00m 192.00m

run.cmd: sudo pvs --units m -o pv_name,vg_name,pv_size,pv_free | grep -E 'PV|labvg' | sed -E 's#/dev/loop[0-9]+#PV#'
run.output:
PV         VG        PSize     PFree 
  PV labvg        96.00m 96.00m
  PV labvg        96.00m 96.00m

steps.title: Create a logical volume and use it
steps.text: `lvcreate -L 40M -n data labvg` makes a 40 MB volume. It appears as `/dev/labvg/data` (a link to `/dev/mapper/labvg-data`). Format and mount it like any disk.

run.cmd: sudo mkfs.ext4 -q /dev/labvg/data; sudo mkdir -p /tmp/lab/lv && sudo mount /dev/labvg/data /tmp/lab/lv && sudo chown $(id -un): /tmp/lab/lv

steps.title: Grow it while it is mounted
steps.text: `lvextend -r -L +60M` adds 60 MB to the volume **and** resizes the file system (`-r`) in one step. Nothing is unmounted and the file is untouched. This is why LVM is popular: running out of space becomes a one-line operation if the VG has free extents.

run.cmd: sudo lvextend -r -L +60M labvg/data 2>&1 | grep -E 'Size of logical volume|resized|Extending'
run.output:
Size of logical volume labvg/data changed from 40.00 MiB (10 extents) to 100.00 MiB (25 extents).
  Extending file system ext4 to 100.00 MiB (104857600 bytes) on labvg/data...
  Logical volume labvg/data successfully resized.

steps.title: Clean up
steps.text: Unmount, then remove from the top down: LV, VG, PV, loop devices.

run.cmd: sudo umount /tmp/lab/lv; sudo lvremove -f labvg/data 2>&1 | tail -n 1; sudo vgremove -f labvg 2>&1 | tail -n 1; sudo pvremove -f $L1 $L2 2>&1 | sed 's#/dev/loop[0-9]*#PV#' | tail -n 2; sudo losetup -d $L1 $L2; echo done
run.output:
Logical volume "data" successfully removed.
  Volume group "labvg" successfully removed
  Labels on physical volume "PV" successfully wiped.
  Labels on physical volume "PV" successfully wiped.
done

steps.under: LVM splits the VG into **extents** (4 MiB by default). An LV is a list of extents, possibly from several PVs. Extending adds extents and then asks the file system to use them (`resize2fs` for ext4, `xfs_growfs` for xfs). Shrinking is the reverse and riskier: shrink the file system first, then the LV.

quiz.q: What are the LVM layers, bottom to top?
quiz.explain: Physical volume, volume group, logical volume.

quiz.q: What does `lvextend -r` do beyond extending the LV?
options: Resizes the file system as well
quiz.explain: The -r flag runs the file system resize.

quiz.q: Where does a logical volume appear?
quiz.explain: Both names point to the device-mapper device.

quiz.q: Which file system cannot be shrunk after `lvreduce` planning?
quiz.explain: xfs cannot shrink, so do not plan to reduce it.

check.scenario: `/var` is at 98% on a server whose root VG has 20 GB free. Give the exact commands to add 10 GB without downtime.
check.answer: `lvs` to find the LV name, then `lvextend -r -L +10G /dev/VG/var` (the `-r` grows the file system, ext4 or xfs, online). Verify with `df -h /var` and `vgs`.

lessons.title: LVM snapshots and the device mapper
lessons.goal:
Take a point-in-time snapshot of a volume, see that it keeps the old data while the original changes, and look at the kernel layer that makes LVM work: the device mapper.

Why it matters: snapshots give consistent backups and quick rollbacks, and `dmsetup` shows what is really mapped when LVM tools misbehave.

setup.note: These steps use sudo and loop devices (image files acting as disks). They create a volume group called `labvg` and remove it at the end. They never touch real disks.

steps.title: Prepare a volume with some data
steps.text: A fresh VG and a 40 MB LV with one file.

run.cmd: truncate -s 200M p1.img; L1=$(sudo losetup -f --show p1.img); sudo pvcreate -q $L1 && sudo vgcreate -q labvg $L1 && sudo lvcreate -q -L 40M -n data labvg
run.output:
Physical volume "/dev/loop0" successfully created.
  Not creating system devices file due to existing VGs.
  Not creating system devices file due to existing VGs.
  Volume group "labvg" successfully created
  Logical volume "data" created.

run.cmd: sudo mkfs.ext4 -q /dev/labvg/data; sudo mkdir -p /tmp/lab/lv /tmp/lab/snap && sudo mount /dev/labvg/data /tmp/lab/lv && sudo chown $(id -un): /tmp/lab/lv; echo 'version 1' > /tmp/lab/lv/config.txt; sync; cat /tmp/lab/lv/config.txt

steps.title: Create a snapshot
steps.text: `lvcreate -s` makes a **copy-on-write snapshot**. It needs space only for blocks that change after the snapshot (here 20 MB). Creating it takes a moment, whatever the size of the origin.

run.cmd: sudo lvs --units m -o lv_name,lv_size,origin,snap_percent labvg | sed 's/  */ /g'
run.output:
LV LSize Origin Snap% 
 before 20.00m data 0.06 
 data 40.00m

steps.title: Change the origin; the snapshot keeps the past
steps.text: We overwrite the file in the origin. The snapshot still shows the old content. Mount it read-only to look.

run.cmd: sudo lvs --units m -o lv_name,snap_percent labvg | sed 's/  */ /g'

steps.after: The snapshot holds `version 1`. `Snap%` grew because the changed blocks were saved there first.

steps.title: Under the hood: device mapper
steps.text: LVM only configures the kernel's **device mapper** (dm). Each LV is a dm device with a **table**: ranges of sectors mapped by a **target** (linear, snapshot, mirror, thin, crypt...). `dmsetup` shows it.

run.cmd: sudo dmsetup ls | grep labvg | sed 's/(.*//' | tr '\n' ' '; echo

steps.under: `linear` means "sectors 0..N of this device map to sectors S..S+N of that device". A snapshot is two targets: `snapshot-origin` (writes to the origin first copy the old block to the snapshot's exception store) and `snapshot` (reads come from the store if the block was copied, else from the origin). The same dm layer implements disk encryption (dm-crypt/LUKS), multipath and thin provisioning.

steps.title: Roll back (merge) or discard
steps.text: To discard a snapshot: `lvremove`. To roll the origin back to the snapshot state use `lvconvert --merge` (done on the next activation of the origin). We just discard and clean up.

run.cmd: sudo umount /tmp/lab/snap /tmp/lab/lv; sudo lvremove -q -f labvg/before labvg/data 2>&1 | tail -n 1; sudo vgremove -q -f labvg; sudo pvremove -q -f $L1; sudo losetup -d $L1; echo cleaned
run.output:
Logical volume "data" successfully removed.
  Volume group "labvg" successfully removed
  Labels on physical volume "/dev/loop0" successfully wiped.
cleaned

quiz.q: What does an LVM snapshot store?
options: A full copy of the volume
Blocks of the origin that changed since the snapshot (copy-on-write)

quiz.q: What happens when a snapshot's space is used up?
quiz.explain: A full classic snapshot is invalidated; monitor Snap%.

quiz.q: What kernel layer implements LVM volumes?
Which tool shows the raw mapping tables?
quiz.explain: dmsetup talks to the device mapper directly.

check.scenario: You must back up a busy database volume consistently with minimal downtime. How do snapshots help and what must you do around them?
check.answer: Quiesce the database briefly (flush/lock, or use its backup mode), create the snapshot (instant), release the lock, then back up from the **mounted read-only snapshot** at leisure, and remove the snapshot afterwards so it does not fill. Size the snapshot for the changes expected during the backup.

interview.a: A physical volume is a disk prepared for LVM, a volume group pools PVs, a logical volume is a slice of the pool that holds a file system. See [the lesson](#/lesson/21/lvm-basics).

interview.q: How do you extend /var online using LVM?
interview.a: `lvextend -r -L +SIZE /dev/VG/var` (the -r resizes ext4 or xfs). Needs free extents in the VG; if none, add a PV with `vgextend` first.

interview.q: How does an LVM snapshot work?
interview.a: Copy-on-write: before an origin block is changed the old data is copied to the snapshot's store. The snapshot sees the old data. See [the lesson](#/lesson/21/lvm-snapshots-devicemapper).
A kernel framework that maps virtual block devices onto other devices through tables and targets (linear, snapshot, crypt, thin, multipath). LVM, LUKS and multipath use it.

commands.desc: Grow an LV and its file system.
